kurz: Munger's 25 tendencies, how they combine in the Lollapalooza effect, and inversion as the only antidote that works when it counts.

bloecke.md:
## How the list came about

In 1995 Charlie Munger gave a talk at Harvard Law School on the causes of human misjudgment. He was a lawyer and not a psychologist, and said so openly. His list, he said, was unsystematic, the points overlapped, and he did not cite evidence from studies. The revised version in *Poor Charlie's Almanack* (2005) comprises 25 tendencies.

The individual cognitive biases are familiar from the previous lessons of this module. This lesson is about three things that the academic list does not provide: an ordering of the errors, how they interact, and an antidote.

Munger's particular contribution is his focus on influences from outside. Behavioural finance describes how people deceive themselves. Munger additionally describes how others deceive them, namely through incentives, authority, reciprocity, reasons and twaddle. Investors have to deal with both: their own fast thinking and a sales industry that has known for decades which of these tendencies it can appeal to.
## The 24 individual tendencies in four groups

zeilen: Reward and punishment superresponse tendency
People do what they are paid for; the question of remuneration explains more recommendations than any argument.
Reciprocation tendency
A gift such as a seminar, a free share or a switching bonus creates the feeling of owing something in return.
Influence-from-mere-association tendency
Qualities are transferred through mere association. Expensive things seem high-quality, and a famous face makes an offer look reputable.
Social-proof tendency
When uncertain, we imitate the majority; this is a major cause of bubbles and panics.
Authority-misinfluence tendency
The judgements of authorities are adopted without scrutiny, from the star fund manager to the finance influencer.
Reason-respecting tendency
A reason markedly increases agreement, even if it is devoid of content.
Liking/loving tendency
With people, brands and companies we like, we overlook flaws and buy their shares uncritically.
Disliking/hating tendency
Conversely, we overlook the strengths of what we reject and pass up investments out of antipathy.
Kantian fairness tendency
Perceived unfairness triggers reactions that run counter to your own financial interest.
Envy/jealousy tendency
Comparison with others steers more decisions than your own goals, even though your neighbour's return is the worst yardstick.
Contrast-misreaction tendency
Amounts are judged relative to the amount next to them, which is why a €1,000 fee looks small next to a €100,000 portfolio.
Doubt-avoidance tendency
The brain ends uncertainty by making a decision, and does so particularly hastily under time pressure.
Inconsistency-avoidance tendency
Opinions, once expressed, are defended, because changing your mind creates inner contradictions.
Simple, pain-avoiding psychological denial
Painful facts are not perceived; that is why many people stop opening their portfolio during a crash.
Excessive self-regard tendency
We consider ourselves, our choices and our possessions to be above average.
Overoptimism tendency
People believe what they wish for; plans and return expectations therefore turn out systematically too optimistic.
Deprival-superreaction tendency
Losing something you own hurts far more than an equally large gain pleases; the reaction is even stronger with narrowly missed opportunities.
Availability-misweighing tendency
What is vivid or currently in the news is overweighted, because what is easy to remember is taken to be frequent.
Curiosity tendency
The only tendency with a predominantly positive effect; it corrects many of the others if you let it.
Stress-influence tendency
Light stress sharpens judgement, heavy stress destroys it; that is why decisions made during a crash are the worst.
Use-it-or-lose-it tendency
Skills wither without practice, and fundamentals that are not applied regularly are lost.
Drug-misinfluence tendency
Alcohol and other substances destroy judgement and encourage denial.
Senescence-misinfluence tendency
Cognitive abilities decline with age at different rates. This argues for simple, automated wealth structures.
Twaddle tendency
People produce a lot of meaningless chatter; a typical example is the daily commentary on price movements.

bloecke.md:
As a whole, the list is not robust. It has never been tested as a whole, the groups overlap, and the numbering indicates a sequence, not a ranking. The individual points are supported by evidence to very different degrees. Social proof and loss aversion have been replicated hundreds of times. No. 12, by contrast, includes the endowment effect, which depends heavily on the experimental design.

Its usefulness lies in the fact that it is short enough to go through before a decision. It is a checklist and not a scientific finding.

## The incentive question (No. 1)

Munger considered the reward and punishment superresponse tendency the most powerful of the 25 tendencies. He counted himself among those who had underestimated it all their lives. For investors in Germany it is above all a matter of sales regulation.

An institution may only accept inducements from product providers if they improve the quality of the service and are disclosed (Section 70 WpHG, Securities Trading Act). It must state the costs in euros before the transaction and, looking back, once a year (Section 63(7) WpHG in conjunction with Article 50 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565). For investment advice to retail clients, Section 64(4) WpHG adds the suitability statement (Geeignetheitserklärung). An adviser who calls themselves a fee-based investment adviser (Honorar-Anlageberater) may not keep inducements (Section 64(5) WpHG). For independent intermediaries, the same dividing line runs between Section 34f GewO (Trade Regulation Act), for commission, and Section 34h GewO, for fees.

The type of authorisation is stated in the legal notice (Impressum). It allows more conclusions to be drawn about the recommendation you can expect than the entire advisory meeting does. An EU-wide ban on commissions has been under discussion for years; you should not count on it.

The sentence “The advice is free of charge for you” is neither a lie nor meaningful. It only says that the investor does not pay directly. Payment is made via the product, out of ongoing charges that reduce the investor's return. Following Munger, you should ask less whether the adviser is reputable than what this person earns from this recommendation and what from the alternative.

European cost statistics show what these incentives cost. According to ESMA analyses, active equity UCITS had ongoing charges of around 1.50% a year over the ten-year period from 2012 to 2021, ETFs 0.31%. Net returns after ongoing and one-off costs were 9.4% and 10.4% a year. This gap follows from arithmetic and is not a forecast. Before costs, the average active return equals the average passive return; after costs, it is necessarily lower (Sharpe, 1991).

bloecke.titel: A difference of 1.0 percentage point in net return over 25 years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with €500 a month and the ESMA net returns (10.4% for ETFs, 9.4% for active equity funds), in which €150,000 of contributions grows to a final value of around €710,000 or around €599,000 respectively.

bloecke.md:
The ongoing charges differ by 1.19 percentage points a year, the net returns by one percentage point. With this difference in return, the two final values are around €111,000 apart after 25 years. That is more than two thirds of all contributions (€150,000).

The gap becomes so large because every euro that flows out as costs earns nothing afterwards. It is missing from compounding for the rest of the term. That is why No. 16, the contrast-misreaction tendency, is particularly dangerous here. Next to a six-figure portfolio value, one percentage point seems insignificant.

## Authority, reasons, twaddle

With the **authority-misinfluence tendency** (No. 22), the test is how often the authority's professional group turns out to be right, and not how convincingly someone comes across. In Morningstar's European Active/Passive Barometer (first half of 2026), only 28.4% of active equity managers had survived and beaten their passive counterpart over one year, and over ten years the figure was just 11.9%. Over long periods, the hit rate of these authorities is therefore well below that of a coin toss.

The **reason-respecting tendency** (No. 24) is demonstrated by Ellen Langer's photocopier experiment of 1978. Compliance with a small request rose from around 60% to over 90% as soon as any reason at all was given, even with the completely empty reason “because I have to make copies”. In sales, half-sentences such as “because of the turn in the interest rate cycle” or “because of demographics” serve the same function. The listener takes note of the reason without examining it.

The daily explanation of price movements (“investors took profits”) is an example of the **twaddle tendency** (No. 23). It is an after-the-fact story with no information content and creates the impression that there is constantly something to decide.

bloecke.md:
## The Lollapalooza effect

Tendency No. 25, the **Lollapalooza effect**, describes the combined action of the other 24. When several of them act in the same direction at the same time, they reinforce one another, and the overall effect is greater than the sum of the individual effects. This is how bubbles, pyramid schemes, panic selling and cults arise, that is, outcomes that could not be explained by any single error on its own.

That is why knowledge about cognitive biases helps so little. A single bias can be neutralised with a counter-question. When four tendencies act at the same time, a choice seems so obviously right that a counter-question achieves nothing at the moment of decision.

bloecke.unter: Six tendencies from different groups lead to the same purchase, and a seventh ensures that it is defended afterwards.

knoten.notiz: Everyone around you is already in

bloecke.md: The Lollapalooza concept has a methodological weakness. In retrospect, every wrong decision can be explained with three or four tendencies, but so can every right decision. An explanation that rules out no outcome permits no prediction. The concept is therefore only useful looking forward, as a warning signal when a decision feels unusually clear-cut. A feeling of complete clarity is no proof of quality. Mostly it indicates that several tendencies are pulling in the same direction.

## Inversion as an antidote

Munger adopted from the mathematician Carl Gustav Jacobi the working rule of inverting difficult problems. Instead of asking how a portfolio becomes successful, you ask what would be sure to ruin it, and then avoid those steps.

Inversion helps against the Lollapalooza effect because it requires a commitment before the decision. All 24 tendencies act on what you feel at the moment of decision, but none of them acts on a sentence you wrote down three weeks earlier.

bloecke.quelle: Carl Gustav Jacobi; made into a decision rule by Charlie Munger

schritte.titel: A ruin list instead of a goal list
schritte.text: Before buying, write down what would turn this position into a permanent loss of capital: cluster risk, foreign currency, the company's debt, balance sheet risk, liquidity. If you cannot name these points, you do not yet understand the position.

Formulate failure as a fact, for example “It is 2031, and the position was a disaster”, and then look for the reasons. Asking for the reasons behind a given outcome demonstrably produces more risks than asking about possible risks.

For every recommendation, find out how the person recommending it is paid. For investment services firms this is stated in the cost information under Section 63(7) WpHG; for intermediaries it is shown by the type of authorisation (Section 34f versus Section 34h GewO).
At least seven days pass between decision and order if the security has been in the headlines in the last 30 days. Time is the only remedy that works against all four groups at once.
Once a year, check whether you would buy this position afresh today at this price. If the answer is no, holding it is a purchase decision that you have just rejected.

bloecke.md:
Buffett and Munger publicly recorded their own mistakes. That too is applied inversion.

- The purchase of Dexter Shoe (1993) ended in a total loss. It was made worse by the fact that Berkshire paid in its own shares, whose value had grown to around $5.7 billion by 2014.
- Buffett bought National Indemnity (1967) through the wrong company. By his own calculation, this cost his partners around $100 billion.
- At Tesco, delayed action after a management problem had been recognised cost $444 million after tax. Munger called this hesitation thumb-sucking.

In the Tesco case, the inconsistency-avoidance tendency (No. 5) and psychological denial (No. 11) worked together. The problem had been recognised, but their own earlier decision delayed the sale.

In a German portfolio, moreover, every correction costs tax. Munger's catalogue does not include this factor. When a position in an equity fund with a book gain of €20,000 is switched, then after the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] (Section 20 InvStG, Investment Tax Act), around 26.375% [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] including solidarity surcharge is due on €14,000 (Section 32d(1) EStG, Income Tax Act). That comes to about €3,690, not counting church tax. Realised losses on shares help only to a limited extent, because they may only be offset against gains from sales of shares (Section 20(6) EStG).

This argues for few, well-founded decisions, but not for sitting out mistakes you have recognised.

The 25 tendencies serve as a checklist before a decision and not as a diagnosis after the fact. The most important check concerns others, namely how the person giving the recommendation is paid. The second most important concerns yourself, namely what would have to happen for the investment to become a disaster.

mitnehmen: Munger adds influences from outside to the academic list, because others can steer your judgement through incentives, authority, reciprocity, reasons and twaddle.

The incentive question comes before all others, and in Germany it can be read from Section 70 WpHG, from the cost information under Section 63(7) WpHG and from the type of authorisation (Section 34f versus Section 34h GewO).
A Lollapalooza arises when several tendencies pull in the same direction, and the feeling of complete clarity is then a warning signal and not a mark of quality.
In retrospect the Lollapalooza concept explains every decision and therefore permits no prediction; it is only useful as an early warning.
Inversion works because it takes place before the emotion; a ruin list, a pre-mortem and a waiting period can no longer be overridden by feelings at the moment of decision.

begriffe.text: Tendency No. 25 in Munger's list. When several cognitive biases act in the same direction at the same time, they reinforce one another and produce extreme outcomes such as bubbles, pyramid schemes or panic selling.

Thinking method after Carl Gustav Jacobi in which a problem is turned around. Instead of asking about the path to success, you ask about the sure path to failure. The method works because it forces a commitment before the decision.

Tendency No. 1 in Munger's list. People align their behaviour with their remuneration more strongly than they themselves believe. With every recommendation, you should therefore check who pays the person recommending it, and for what.
Tendency No. 24 in Munger's list. A request or recommendation meets with markedly more agreement as soon as it is followed by any “because” at all, even if the reason is devoid of content.

Tendency No. 16 in Munger's list. Amounts are judged relative to the comparison value next to them instead of in absolute terms. That is why ongoing charges look harmless next to a large portfolio value.
Exercise in which you assume that a project has already failed and look for the causes. It produces more risks, and more concrete ones, than the open question about possible risks.
